frames.narration: A scheduler keeps 1,000 tasks in an unsorted array: push is free, but every pop scans all of them. Pushing and popping everything costs 501,500 steps. A sorted array moves the cost to the pushes: 246,079.

A binary heap keeps only a partial order: every parent is no larger than its children, so the smallest is at position 0. Push climbs past larger parents, pop sinks the last item from the root. Both cost about log2 n: 17,194 steps for the same 1,000 tasks.

All 10,000 items are already in hand. Pushing them one by one costs 113,631 comparisons when they arrive in descending order, since each one climbs to the top. Sifting every parent down, last parent first, costs 19,982: under 2n, because half of the nodes are leaves.
Top-k: keep a heap of the k largest and compare each new item with its root. For 10 of 10,000 shuffled items that is 10,285 comparisons, against 120,463 to sort everything.

Break it: ask for the top 100 and feed the items in ascending order. Every new item beats the root and sinks, so the heap needs 123,566 comparisons, more than the full sort at 120,463. A heap of k wins when most items are dropped at the door.

A shortest-path search lowers a queued item's priority. The heap cannot find it without a scan, and scanning for each of 1,000 updates costs 684,633 steps in all. A position index finds it directly: 17,707 comparisons.
Without an index, push a duplicate with the new priority and skip stale entries when they surface: 37,818 comparisons, but the heap grew to 2,000 entries for 1,000 items.

Strict priority starves. A priority-9 task waits since tick 0 while one more urgent task arrives and is served each tick: it did not run within 2000 ticks. Keying the heap by priority times 10 plus arrival tick lets it climb a level every 10 ticks, and it runs at tick 43.

states.consumer: serves the priority-9 task at tick 43
